recent.question: San Diego wins
recent.what_happened: The Padres beat the Cubs 8-0 in Game 1 of the NL Wild Card Series at Petco Park. Tatis and Machado homered in the first inning, and Padres pitching, led by Michael King, held Chicago to one hit.
recent.what_we_missed: Our 0.39 bet heavily against a market at 0.545 because of thin evidence: a six-game regular-season series and a small sample of road teams winning early Wild Card Series. We gave too little weight to San Diego's home field, its 17-3 finish, its top offense since Sept. 1, and King's strong recent form against Boyd's weaker season numbers.
recent.lesson: In a single playoff game between evenly matched teams, don't move more than a few points away from the market because of a small regular-season head-to-head record or a base rate built on about 12 series.

suggested_change.change: When the market price is near 50/50 in a single-game sports market, cap how far the forecast can differ from it (for example, ±7 points) unless there is concrete new information such as a lineup or pitching change or an injury, not just historical head-to-head records.

recent.question: Will Trump say "Piggy" before Oct 1, 2026?
recent.what_happened: The market resolved YES: Trump said "piggy" in some form before the Oct 1, 2026 deadline. My searches did not find the exact remark. The "piggy bank" trade line he has used for years is the most likely source; a new insult is less likely. With about two days left, the market priced YES at 61%. The forecaster said 41%, and both betting strategies lost about $2,000 each on NO.
recent.what_we_missed: The research looked mostly for "piggy" used as an insult to reporters and put little weight on how often Trump says "piggy bank" when talking about tariffs and trade. It also didn't check full transcripts, such as Factba.se or Roll Call, where passing uses of the word turn up. The forecaster had no specific information to justify staying 20 points below the market.
recent.lesson: For mention markets, count every phrase that contains the word (here "piggy bank"), not just its best-known use. Don't bet well below the market price without concrete evidence that the market has it wrong.

suggested_change.change: For word-mention questions, list the compound phrases Trump commonly uses that contain the target word, estimate how often he says them, and search transcript archives like Factba.se for recent uses before departing from the market price.

recent.question: Las Vegas wins
recent.what_happened: Indiana beat Las Vegas 99-89 at home in Game 2 on Sept 29, 2026, which forced a deciding Game 3 in Las Vegas.
recent.what_we_missed: Nothing that could have been known beforehand. But the research-backed forecast (0.62) went well above the market (0.475) mostly because of Game 1's blowout and the Aces' winning streak. That gave too little weight to Indiana's home court, the Fever winning 2 of 3 regular-season meetings, and how often teams bounce back after losing a series opener.
recent.lesson: In playoff series, don't let one lopsided game or a winning streak push you far from a near-even market price when the other team is at home and has a winning head-to-head record.

suggested_change.change: Pull the research forecast back toward the market when the edge rests mostly on recent-game momentum rather than new information such as injuries or lineup changes.

recent.question: Chicago WS wins
recent.what_happened: The White Sox won Game 1 by 6-3 in Houston. Both teams used bullpen games, and Chicago came out ahead. The market had the White Sox near 46.5%, and the forecast without research was 46%, but after research the forecast fell to 28%.
recent.what_we_missed: The research moved us far below the market on weak evidence. It leaned on a 7-game head-to-head record that the sources couldn't even agree on (5-2 vs '5 of 6'). It also used 4 scoreless innings from Blubaugh and the 2021 playoff history. Meanwhile it underweighted the fact that Chicago had the better record (84-78 vs 81-81) and that road teams had won 8 of 12 Wild Card Series.
recent.lesson: In a single baseball game with two roughly even teams and a market near 50/50, small-sample head-to-head records and old playoff history shouldn't move the forecast more than a few points from the market.

suggested_change.change: Flag or cap any forecast on a single MLB game that is more than 10 points away from a market priced between 40% and 60%, unless the research turns up concrete new information such as a confirmed injury or lineup change.

recent.question: Houston wins
recent.what_happened: In a matchup of bullpen games, the White Sox beat the Astros 6-3 in Game 1 at Daikin Park. Colson Montgomery homered to make it 4-0, and Nelson Velázquez's 2-run homer in the 5th was the only real answer Houston had.
recent.what_we_missed: The research-backed forecast of 0.64 was well above the market's 0.535, and the evidence behind it was weak. Chicago had the better record (84-78 vs 81-81). The head-to-head record was small and the summary contradicted itself (5-2 vs '5 of 6'). Blubaugh's 4 scoreless innings is a tiny sample, and in bullpen games the opener matters less. The base rate we had even favored road teams in Wild Card series (8 of 12).
recent.lesson: In a single playoff game between two roughly even teams, stay close to the market. Don't move 10 or more points away based on small head-to-head samples or a few innings from an opener.

suggested_change.change: Cap how far a forecast can move from the market on near-coin-flip MLB single games unless there is concrete new information, like a lineup or injury change the market hasn't priced in.

recent.question: Bari: Completed Match: Massimo Giunta vs Federico Arnaboldi
recent.what_happened: Giunta and Arnaboldi played their first-round Bari Challenger match on 29 September 2026 as scheduled. It went to a normal finish with no retirement or walkover, so the market resolved Yes.
recent.what_we_missed: Most ATP Challenger matches finish normally, about 93–96% of the time. Nothing in our facts pointed to an injury or withdrawal. The researched forecast (0.48) put too much weight on vague worries: Arnaboldi played three qualifying matches, one opponent retired against him, and the ATP page hadn't posted a result yet, even though the match hadn't started. It ended up below both the market (0.71) and the forecast made without research (0.93).
recent.lesson: For 'match completed' markets, start from the roughly 95% completion base rate and only move well below it when there's specific evidence, like a reported injury, a withdrawal, or a player retiring in their previous match. General fatigue or a result not yet posted isn't enough.

suggested_change.change: Block any match-completion forecast below 0.80 unless the research cites a specific injury, withdrawal, or retirement by one of the two players in this event.

recent_wins.question: Boston wins
recent_wins.what_happened: The Yankees beat the Red Sox 9-0 in Game 1 of the AL Wild Card Series at Yankee Stadium. Cam Schlittler struck out 10 over six shutout innings, and Payton Tolle gave up one run in 4⅔ innings before the Yankees pulled away against Boston's bullpen.
recent_wins.what_worked: The research turned up the lopsided starting-pitcher matchup (Schlittler's AL-leading 1.95 ERA and 215 ERA+ against a rookie), Boston's .579 OPS against the Yankees this season, and the Red Sox being outscored 34-15 at Yankee Stadium. Together these moved the forecast from 0.48 without research to 0.24, well below the market's 0.445. Even so, any single playoff game is noisy, and a 9-0 margin says more about the size of the edge than how sure we should have been.
recent_wins.lesson: In single playoff games with a big starting-pitcher gap and a strong head-to-head split, trust the matchup-specific numbers over a hazy 'road teams win Game 1' base rate recalled from memory.

suggested_change.change: Treat base-rate counts the research desk flags as 'from memory, source disagreed' as unverified. Check them against a source or leave them out, instead of letting them pull the forecast toward the underdog.

recent_wins.question: Minnesota wins
recent_wins.what_happened: The No. 8 seed Liberty beat the No. 1 seed Lynx 87-71 at Barclays Center on Sept 29. Minnesota never led, so New York swept the best-of-three series 2-0 and Minnesota was eliminated.
recent_wins.what_worked: Research pulled in the matchup-specific evidence: New York's 16-point road win in Game 1, its 3-1 edge in the 2026 head-to-head, Stewart's dominance, Miles's poor return from injury and the Lynx's 0-3 franchise record after losing Game 1. Together these moved the forecast from 0.49 without research to 0.23. The market stayed at 0.595 because it kept anchoring on Minnesota's 33-11 seed and 17-4 road record. Still, this was one playoff game, and a forecast of 0.23 means Minnesota wins about one time in four, so part of the good result is variance.
recent_wins.lesson: In a short playoff series between two strong teams, give more weight to direct head-to-head results and the most recent game than to regular-season record or seeding, especially when the lower seed has a strong record for its seed and a fresh blowout win.

suggested_change.change: Always collect head-to-head results from the current season and margins from earlier games in the series, and flag when the market's favorite is based mainly on seeding or overall record.

recent_wins.question: New York vs Minnesota First Round series winner: Minnesota wins
recent_wins.what_happened: New York beat Minnesota 87-71 in Game 2 at Barclays Center on Sept. 29. The No. 8 Liberty swept the No. 1 Lynx 2-0 and the market resolved NO.
recent_wins.what_worked: After research, the forecast dropped from 0.43 to 0.31. It weighed three things: Minnesota had to win two straight games, one of them on the road; New York won Game 1 by 16 behind a dominant Breanna Stewart; and since 2022, teams that lose Game 1 of a best-of-three have rarely come back. The market sat at 0.435, still pricing Minnesota as the top seed rather than as a team trailing 1-0. The call was right in direction, but a 31% chance was never a long shot, so part of this was variance.
recent_wins.lesson: Once a best-of-three series is 1-0, price the trailing team as needing to win two straight games, one of them away, and discount their regular-season seeding. That usually puts them below 40%, and the market tends to hold on to the seeding.

suggested_change.change: For best-of-three series with a 1-0 lead, always pull the modern-format (2022+) comeback rate and compare it to the market, rather than relying on older 2010–2015 counts that make comebacks look more common.

recent_wins.question: 1st inning: Over 0.5 runs
recent_wins.what_happened: In the top of the 1st, Kyle Schwarber drew a one-out walk against Chris Sale, and Alec Bohm drove him in with a two-out, 2-2-count double, so the Phillies led 1-0. That made the question resolve YES. Luzardo then threw a scoreless 10-pitch bottom of the 1st.
recent_wins.what_worked: Not much specific reasoning carried it. Our 0.56 was above both the league base rate the forecaster had (about 45% of games have a first-inning run) and the market's 0.415, even though two aces were pitching (Sale had a 2.16 ERA, and Luzardo's last start against Atlanta was a shutout). The only run came from a walk plus a two-out double with two strikes, which is close to a coin flip.
recent_wins.lesson: If a playoff game has an ace on each side and our number is above both the league base rate and the market, that needs a specific reason. A YES result doesn't show the edge was real.

suggested_change.change: When the forecast moves from the base rate toward the side that the pitching facts argue against, cut the bet size or require a written reason before betting on first-inning run markets.

recent_wins.question: Will there be more than 30 transit calls through the Strait of Hormuz from Sep 21, 2026 to Sep 27, 2026? (Above 30)
recent_wins.what_happened: The market resolved NO: IMF PortWatch counted 30 or fewer transit calls through Hormuz for Sep 21–27, 2026. Throughput stayed near 1% of normal after Trump rejected Iran's reopening proposal on Sep 27. PortWatch's Sep 21–27 daily figures were still unpublished in the sources I checked on Sep 29, so I couldn't confirm the exact total. Other trackers reported higher counts because they include dark (AIS-off) transits, e.g. Windward's 24 vessels on Sep 27 and 55 transits over Sep 16–23.
recent_wins.what_worked: The research anchored on PortWatch's own recent numbers: 78 transits over Sep 1–20 (about 27 a week), 8 on Sep 13 and 1 on Sep 20. It also noted that PortWatch is AIS-based and misses dark transits, so it discounted the higher Windward, Reuters and US-official counts. That moved the forecast from 42% without research to 15%, below the market's 20.5%.
recent_wins.lesson: When a question resolves on a specific data source, forecast from that source's recent run rate and how it counts. Treat other trackers' higher figures as noise unless they use the same method, here AIS-visible transits only.

suggested_change.change: For count questions tied to one data provider, always pull that provider's trailing 2–4 week totals and write down its counting rules, such as AIS-only, before looking at other sources.

recent_wins.question: Will Sweden win on 2026-09-28?
recent_wins.what_happened: Sweden beat Poland 3-1 at Strawberry Arena on 28 September 2026. Nygren scored in the 8th minute, Szymański equalised in the 43rd, and Ayari (63') and Gyökeres (72') won it for Sweden, who now have two wins from two in Nations League B Group 4. Sweden won within 90 minutes, so the market resolved YES.
recent_wins.what_worked: The research took the forecast from 0.35 to 0.55, about 10 points above the market's 0.445. The main reasons were Sweden playing at home, their 5-2 head-to-head record including a 3-2 win at the same ground in March, Poland failing to score against Bosnia, and Poland losing Kaminski. Even so, 55% is close to a coin flip on a result that had three possible outcomes, and Sweden were missing Isak, Holm and Ekdal. The evidence leaned the right way, but the outcome itself was largely luck.
recent_wins.lesson: When a home side has a clear head-to-head record against the same opponent, recent wins at the same venue and better current form, and its opponent is struggling to score, give those facts a few points of weight over the market even if the home side has headline injuries. Their depth may cover the missing players.

suggested_change.change: Before discounting a team for injuries, check who replaces the injured players and whether the team has won without them before (here Nygren, Ayari and Gyökeres covered for Isak), rather than treating a star's absence as a large penalty by default.

rules.rule: For short-window crypto price questions, record a spot price from the exchange and pair named in the resolution rules (e.g. Binance BTC/USDT), taken as close to judgment time as possible, and state its timestamp and age.

For crypto threshold questions, report the percent distance from current spot to the strike, the hours left in the window, and recent realized volatility over a similar span, noting whether the window falls on a usually quieter weekend.

Read the resolution rules to see whether a crypto question needs any touch of the level during the window or a close at a specific candle and time, and measure the current price against that exact test.

Do not treat earlier-week touches of a level or prior days' closes as evidence about the current window; identify what drove those moves (e.g. a weekday bond-yield spike) and check whether that driver is still active now.

For short-horizon crypto questions, search same-day macro and geopolitical news (dollar, bond yields, oil, major policy statements) and report any specific catalyst with timestamps, or state plainly that none was found.
For single-match win questions, read the resolution rules to confirm whether only a win in regulation time counts, and state plainly that a draw would resolve No.

For match questions, report the full head-to-head record between the two teams and each side's confirmed suspensions and injuries, citing dated team, federation or reputable news sources for each absence.
Discard any search snippet claiming a match result that is undated or dated before kickoff; report a result only from sources published after the match was played.

For tennis 'completed match' questions, read which endings count as not completed (retirement, walkover), and report the historical share of matches finished through normal play at that tour level (WTA 125, ATP Challenger) as the starting reference.

For tennis completion questions, report as risk evidence only specific, dated news from the past week: an injury, a withdrawal, or a retirement at this event; label old retirements, back-to-back events or qualifying load, and a result not yet posted as weak context.

Just before a tennis match, check the tournament's latest order of play, draw updates and withdrawal lists for walkovers, late withdrawals or lucky-loser swaps, and report recent full matches each player finished (singles or doubles) as fitness evidence.

When a count question resolves on one named data provider, pull that provider's own trailing 2–4 week figures and write down its counting method (e.g. AIS-visible only) first; set aside other trackers' figures that count differently.

proposals.title: Break results down by price paid
proposals.why: Many losses, including all 3 of claude_direct's and every info-gate-stopped group, show -$100 per $100, meaning the whole stake was lost. That pattern suggests we may be buying cheap longshots. A breakdown of wins and P&L by ask price (for example <0.2, 0.2–0.5, 0.5–0.8, >0.8), for placed and stopped bets, would let us set min_ask and max_ask from evidence instead of guessing.
proposals.judge_by: The review data includes a by-price breakdown, and within 2 reviews it leads to either a min_ask/max_ask tune or a clear finding that price doesn't matter.

proposals.title: Claude direct, pickier and without crypto
proposals.why: Claude is our best forecaster (Brier 0.132 on 24) yet lost all 3 of its settled bets. The places where it disagrees with the market by only 8% are probably where the market is right. This challenger demands a 12% edge, skips crypto, and bets half as much per bet.
proposals.judge_by: Positive P&L, and more P&L per $100 staked than claude_direct over the same period.
proposals.status_reason: started automatically within the allowed bounds

proposals.title: Bold meets the info gate halfway
proposals.why: Bold's extra bets, where Jev's info rating is 0.2–0.5, are losing $31.79 per $100 (7 bets), and main's info-stopped markets lose $70 per $100 (16). A 0.35 threshold tests where the cutoff really belongs, without collapsing bold into a copy of main.
proposals.judge_by: Bold's P&L per $100 staked since the change beats its old -$31.79 per $100, and is closer to or above main's over the same period.

proposals.title: Main skips crypto
proposals.why: In crypto the market scores a Brier of 0.034 against Jev+research's 0.117 (9 resolved), so any edge we think we see there is most likely our own error. This is an experiment on a small sample.

retro.headline: Day one: the market's own price is still the best forecaster (Brier 0.116 vs 0.132 for Claude and 0.157 for Jev+research); main is up $1,867 on just 5 settled bets, the loosened strategies are down about $6k each, and the info gate is the one filter that is clearly paying off.
went_well: Main is up $1,866.73 (3 wins, 2 losses on 5 settled, 7 still open). That is too few to call a finding. Against original, which runs identical rules, the yardstick is a tie: +$489 vs +$473 on 2 settled bets. That is expected, since nothing has been tuned yet.

The info gate is saving money everywhere we can see it. Markets it alone stopped would have lost $70–$88 per $100: main 16 stopped with 2 wins, jev_alone 37 with 3 wins, jev_alone_bold 21 with 1 win, claude_direct 8 with 1 win. These strategies look at many of the same markets, so this is fewer inde
Claude direct is the best of our forecasters, with a Brier of 0.132 on 24 resolved (lower is better). Jev with research scores 0.157 on 44.
went_badly: Nothing we have beats the market. Its price scores 0.116 on 69 resolved. It is far ahead in crypto (0.034 vs Jev+research 0.117 on 9) and ahead in sports (0.141 vs 0.177 on 30).
Jev alone scores 0.262 on 69 resolved, which is worse than always guessing 50% (0.25). With 69 results this is a real finding, not noise.

Claude direct went 0 for 3 on settled bets (-$6,000). Bold went 2–6 on 8 settled (-$5,898), and its extra bets, taken where Jev's info rating was 0.2–0.5, are losing $31.79 per $100. Both samples are tiny.

rule_changes.why: Bold's extra bets, where Jev's info rating is 0.2–0.5, are losing $31.79 per $100 (7 bets), and main's info-stopped markets lose $70 per $100 (16). A 0.35 threshold tests where the cutoff really belongs, without collapsing bold into a copy of main.
rule_changes.judge_by: Bold's P&L per $100 staked since the change beats its old -$31.79 per $100, and is closer to or above main's over the same period.

rule_changes.judge_by: On the yardstick, main's P&L on bets opened after this change is at least original's. Meanwhile, original's crypto bets over the same period lose money in total.

ideas_for_joey.title: Break results down by price paid
ideas_for_joey.why: Many losses, including all 3 of claude_direct's and every info-gate-stopped group, show -$100 per $100, meaning the whole stake was lost. That pattern suggests we may be buying cheap longshots. A breakdown of wins and P&L by ask price (for example <0.2, 0.2–0.5, 0.5–0.8, >0.8), for placed and stopped bets, would let us set min_ask and max_ask from evidence instead of guessing.
